summary.text: Writing the continued fraction as \(X_2/X_3\), its recurrence and a conserved Casoratian give \(X_2=(n+1)^2-5\) and \((n-2)X_3-U_3X_2=2(n-1)!\). Quadratic reciprocity supplies a suitably bounded even \(m\) with \(m^2\equiv5\pmod p\); setting \(n=m-1\) and \(t=(m^2-5)/p\), parity and the factorization \((m-3)(m+3)=pt-4\) give \(\gcd(n-2,t)=1\), and the Casoratian identity then shows that reduction cancels exactly \(t\), leaving denominator \(p\).

full_proof.text: Let \[ R_{n-1}=(n-1)-\frac n{-4}=(n-1)+\frac n4, \qquad R_k=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}}\quad(2\le k\le n-2). \] Thus the continued fraction in the definition of the sequence is \(1/R_2\). If \(R_2=N/D\) in lowest terms, then \(1/R_2=D/N\), so the reduced denominator \(a(n)\) is \(|N|\). We shall prove that every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) can be made equal to this reduced numerator. ## 1. Integer continuants for the continued fraction Fix \(n\ge3\). Define integers \(X_k\), for \(2\le k\le n\), backward by \[ X_n=4, \qquad X_{n-1}=5n-4, \] and \[ X_k=kX_{k+1}-(k+1)X_{k+2} \qquad(2\le k\le n-2). \] The choice of the two terminal values reflects \[ R_{n-1}=(n-1)+\frac n4=\frac{5n-4}{4} =\frac{X_{n-1}}{X_n}. \] We first establish positivity, in particular ensuring that none of the denominators introduced below vanishes. We claim that for every \(2\le k\le n-1\), \[ X_k>0 \quad\text{and}\quad (k-1)X_k>k(k-2)X_{k+1}. \tag{1} \] At \(k=n-1\), positivity follows from \(X_{n-1}=5n-4>0\), and the inequality is \[ (n-2)(5n-4)>4(n-1)(n-3). \] The difference between the two sides is \[ n^2+2n-4>0 \] for \(n\ge3\), so the initial case holds. Now suppose (1) holds at \(k+1\). Its inequality there is \[ kX_{k+1}>(k+1)(k-1)X_{k+2}. \tag{2} \] Using the recurrence for \(X_k\), we calculate that the desired inequality at \(k\) is equivalent to \[ (k-1)\bigl(kX_{k+1}-(k+1)X_{k+2}\bigr) >k(k-2)X_{k+1}, \] which, after collecting terms, is exactly (2). Furthermore, the right-hand side of the desired inequality is nonnegative because \(k\ge2\) and \(X_{k+1}>0\). Hence \((k-1)X_k>0\), and since \(k-1>0\), we also get \(X_k>0\). This proves (1) by backward induction. Together with \(X_n=4>0\), all the \(X_k\) are positive. It now follows by backward induction that \[ R_k=\frac{X_k}{X_{k+1}} \qquad(2\le k\le n-1). \tag{3} \] We already checked the terminal case. If the statement holds at \(k+1\), then, using the positivity just proved to justify division, \[ R_k =k-\frac{k+1}{X_{k+1}/X_{k+2}} =\frac{kX_{k+1}-(k+1)X_{k+2}}{X_{k+1}} =\frac{X_k}{X_{k+1}}. \] In particular, \[ R_2=\frac{X_2}{X_3}. \tag{4} \] ## 2. Three Casoratian identities We need an explicit formula for \(X_2\) and a divisibility relation involving \(X_3\). Introduce a second integer solution \(U_k\) of the same recurrence: \[ U_n=0, \qquad U_{n-1}=1, \qquad U_k=kU_{k+1}-(k+1)U_{k+2}. \] Also define the rational sequence \[ S_j=\frac{j-2}{(j-1)!}. \] A direct calculation using \((j+1)!= (j+1)j(j-1)!\) shows that \[ S_j=jS_{j+1}-(j+1)S_{j+2}. \tag{5} \] Moreover, \[ S_2=0, \qquad S_3=\frac12. \] For any two sequences \(A_j,B_j\) satisfying the recurrence \[ Y_j=jY_{j+1}-(j+1)Y_{j+2}, \] define their factorial-weighted Casoratian by \[ W_j(A,B)=j!\bigl(A_jB_{j+1}-A_{j+1}B_j\bigr). \] This quantity is independent of \(j\). Indeed, substituting the recurrence for \(A_j\) and \(B_j\) gives \[ \begin{aligned} A_jB_{j+1}-A_{j+1}B_j &=\bigl(jA_{j+1}-(j+1)A_{j+2}\bigr)B_{j+1}\\ &\quad-A_{j+1}\bigl(jB_{j+1}-(j+1)B_{j+2}\bigr)\\ &=(j+1)\bigl(A_{j+1}B_{j+2}-A_{j+2}B_{j+1}\bigr). \end{aligned} \] Multiplying by \(j!\) proves \(W_j=W_{j+1}\). Apply this first to \(X\) and \(S\). At the lower end, \[ W_2(X,S) =2!\left(X_2\cdot\frac12-X_3\cdot0\right)=X_2. \] At the upper end, \[ \begin{aligned} W_{n-1}(X,S) &=(n-1)!\left(X_{n-1}S_n-X_nS_{n-1}\right)\\ &=(n-1)!\left((5n-4)\frac{n-2}{(n-1)!} -4\frac{n-3}{(n-2)!}\right)\\ &=(5n-4)(n-2)-4(n-1)(n-3)\\ &=n^2+2n-4. \end{aligned} \] Constancy of the Casoratian therefore gives \[ X_2=n^2+2n-4=(n+1)^2-5. \tag{6} \] Apply the same argument to \(U\) and \(S\). We have \[ W_2(U,S)=U_2, \] while \[ W_{n-1}(U,S) =(n-1)!\left(1\cdot\frac{n-2}{(n-1)!} -0\cdot\frac{n-3}{(n-2)!}\right) =n-2. \] Thus \[ U_2=n-2. \tag{7} \] Finally, apply the Casoratian identity to \(X\) and \(U\). At the upper end, \[ W_{n-1}(X,U) =(n-1)!\bigl((5n-4)\cdot0-4\cdot1\bigr) =-4(n-1)!. \] At the lower end, using (7), \[ W_2(X,U) =2\bigl(X_2U_3-X_3U_2\bigr) =2\bigl(X_2U_3-(n-2)X_3\bigr). \] Equating these expressions and dividing by \(-2\) yields the fundamental relation \[ (n-2)X_3-U_3X_2=2(n-1)!. \tag{8} \] ## 3. A criterion ensuring that \(a(n)=p\) Suppose that \(p\) is prime and that positive integers \(n,t\) satisfy \[ n\ge3, \tag{9} \] \[ (n+1)^2-5=pt, \tag{10} \] \[ 02\). Thus the prime \(p\) divides neither \(2\) nor \((n-1)!\), a contradiction. Write \(X_3=tD\), possible by (16). Positivity of \(X_3\) and \(t\) shows \(D>0\). Equation (17) shows \(p\nmid D\), and therefore \(\gcd(p,D)=1\). By (4) and (14), \[ R_2=\frac{X_2}{X_3}=\frac{pt}{tD}=\frac pD. \] This last fraction is in lowest terms. Hence its numerator is \(p\), and the reciprocal continued fraction \(1/R_2=D/p\) has reduced denominator \(p\). Therefore \[ a(n)=p. \tag{18} \] It remains to construct \(n,t\) satisfying (9)--(13). ## 4. Choosing an even square root of \(5\) modulo \(p\) We first work under the slightly more general assumptions that \(p\) is prime, \[ p\ne2,5, \qquad p\equiv1\text{ or }4\pmod5. \tag{19} \] We use the standard quadratic reciprocity theorem: for distinct odd primes \(r,s\), \[ \left(\frac rs\right)\left(\frac sr\right) =(-1)^{((r-1)/2)((s-1)/2)}. \] Since \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), this gives \[ \left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right). \] The nonzero squares modulo \(5\) are \(1\) and \(4\). Assumption (19) therefore says that \(p\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(5\), and quadratic reciprocity implies that \(5\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\).
